articles.title: Theni jailbreak: Efforts are on to nab escaped prisoners who are still absconding, says T.N. Law Minister Nirmal Kumar
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: Tamil Nadu Minister for Energy Resources and Law C.T.R. Nirmal Kumar, speaking to reporters in Coimbatore on Tuesday (October 27, 2026), said efforts are under way to nab 13 of the 17 prisoners who escaped from District Jail at Thekkampatti in Theni district the previous night.

Commenting on the jailbreak in which 17 remand prisoners escaped from the prison after they allegedly assaulted three prison guards, the Minister said four of them had been arrested and efforts were under way to trace and apprehend the remaining 13 prisoners.

Checks have been intensified at checkpoints including those along the Kerala border and in forest areas. Director-General of Prisons and Correctional Services Sandeep Rai Rathore and the Inspector-General of Police are inspecting in person to ascertain whether there had been any security lapses, the Minister added.

Further, responding to former Chief Minister and DMK president M.K. Stalin’s allegation that the arrest of former School Education Minister Anbil Mahesh Poyyamozhi was an act of political vendetta, the Minister rejected the claims. He said the investigation into the allegations against Mr. Poyyamozhi would proceed according to law.
Mr. Nirmal Kumar alleged that more than ₹400 crores had been collected from schools in the name of ‘party funds’ through a certificate related to school safety during Mr. Poyyamozhi’s tenure

He also accused the DMK of threatening educational institutions into making payments. He claimed that schools run by non-governmental organisations, Christian missionary groups and trusts had also faced pressure and said more institutions were now coming forward to lodge complaints.

Referring to remark — “they should have finished him off in Karur that very day” — allegedly made by Mr. Poyyamozhi’s supporters outside the court in Chennai, the Minister alleged that the statement raised questions about possible prior planning in connection with the 2025 Karur stampede.

On the death of Coimbatore school student A. Akilan by suicide , he said the police had been given a free hand to investigate the case and that there would be no political pressure. He said anyone found to have committed a crime would be dealt with in accordance with the law.

On rooftop solar installations, Mr. Nirmal Kumar said Tamil Nadu had installed 87,000 systems by April and had received more than 27,000 applications in the subsequent five months. The government aimed to install rooftop solar systems in one lakh houses by March (2027), with around 10,000 applications already processed.

He also said the government was reviewing fixed electricity charges and would announce the outcome of its assessment within a week. Long-term power purchase agreements for more than 4,000 MW were planned, subject to approval from the Tamil Nadu Electricity Regulatory Commission.

articles.title: Cylone ‘Arnab’: Visakhapatnam, Srikakulam districts in A.P. receive widespread rainfall
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: As cyclone ‘Arnab’ moves closer to the coast, many parts of Srikakulam and Visakhapatnam districts in north Andhra Pradesh continue to receive widespread rainfall on Tuesday (October 27, 2026).

The India Meteorological Department (IMD), Amaravati, and Cylone Warning Centre, Visakhapatnam, have issued a red alert for the districts of Srikakulam, Parvathipuram Manyam, Vizianagaram, Visakhapatnam, Alluri Sitharama Raju, Anakapalli and Kakinada, as isolated extremely rainfall is likely in these places in the next three hours until 4 p.m. on Tuesday (October 27, 2026).

Between 8.30 a.m. and 1 p.m. on Tuesday (October 27, 2026), Visakhapatnam Rural recorded 57.9 mm, the Jathara premises area recorded 50.25 mm, Tulasi Nagar park area recorded 47.6 mm, Kapuluppada area in Bheemunipatnam recorded 47.5 mm, Government Eye Hospital area in Seethammadhara recorded 45.93 mm, Commonpoint area in Maharanipeta recorded 45.5 mm. All these are in Visakhapatnam district.
Other places in Visakhapatnam, Srikakulam, Vizianagaram, Anakapalli and Parvathipuram Manyam districts recorded less than 45 mm.
In Kakinada and Dr. B.R. Ambedkar Konaseema districts, where the landfall is likely to happen, not much rainfall activity has been reported yet.

Meanwhile, the very severe cyclonic storm over west central Bay of Bengal moved nearly west-northwestwards with a speed of 20 kmph and lay centered at around 220 km south-southeast of Vishakhapatnam, 240 km east-southeast of Kakinada, 340 km east-southeast of Machilipatnam, 370 km south of Gopalpur of Odisha and 410 km east of Bapatla.

There is also a trough that runs from southwest Bay of Bengal, off Sri Lanka coast, to the centre of the storm.

Squally weather with wind speed reaching 40-50 kmph is prevailing over the coast in the districts of Anakapalli, Vishakhapatnam, Kakinada, East Godavari, West Godavari, Konaseema, Krishna, Bapatla from Tuesday morning (October 27, 2026). It could increase gradually, reaching 60-70 kmph by Tuesday afternoon, the IMD said.

articles.title: Theni jailbreak: Human error led to escape of prisoners, says DGP-Prisons Sandeep Rai Rathore; nine guards suspended
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: A ‘human error’ led to the escape of 17 inmates from the Theni district jail on Monday (October 26, 2026) night, Director-General of Police, Prisons, Sandeep Rai Rathore, said.

While four of the escaped prisoners were already secured, an intensive combing operation was under way in Theni district and adjoining areas to apprehend the others. The State authorities were in touch with their counterpart in Keralam to mount vigil on all roads leading to the inter-State borders.
17 remand prisoners escape from sub-jail in Theni district; combing operations lead to arrest of four: IGP
Theni jailbreak: Efforts are on to nab escaped prisoners who are still absconding, says T.N. Law Minister Nirmal Kumar
The inmates, five of whom were involved in a sensational murder case in Vikramangalam police station limits in Madurai district, overpowered jail warders and escaped through the main entry.

“There was a clear breach of security protocol as the prisoners managed to pass through a three-tier barrier manned by security personnel. Some prison staff were carried away by the claim that an inmate had suffered epilepsy and was battling for life. Their focus was on shifting him to the hospital. The prisoners took advantage of this gap and escaped,” Dr. Rathore told The Hindu on Tuesday (October 27).
Nine prison guards in different ranks were placed under suspension.

The DGP said a detailed inquiry had been ordered into the lapses and circumstances that led to the escape of the prisoners, and firm action would be taken against the staff found guilty of dereliction of duty. Parrying questions on the possibility of some prison officials colluding with the accused prisoners, he said any such nexus would be known only after the inquiry.

Dr. Rathore said a security audit of all prisons in Tamil Nadu was ordered soon after the escape of a Nepali prisoner in Puzhal central prison recently. It came to light that the electrified fence had been defunct for quite some time.

“A gap analysis is under way in all prison complexes across the State. Prisons are hardened targets where foolproof security arrangements should be in place…there should be no room for any complacency,” he said.

“Soon after the escape of prisoners was reported, we alerted senior officers in South and Central Zone to conduct vehicle checks and enhance surveillance in railway stations, bus stands, etc. We are working in coordination with the DGP of Keralam in the search operations,” Dr. Aggarwal said.

articles.title: Cyclone ‘Arnab’ LIVE updates | Storm 170 km from Visakhapatnam; landfall near Yanam; Nepal on high alert
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: The rain on Tuesday did not stop the campaign for the November 1 local body polls in Visakhapatnam. YSRCP candidate B. Vijaya Lakshmi went round Ward 40 at One Town in a raincoat with former MLA Vasupalli Ganesh Kumar.

Cyclone Arnab was about 170 km out at sea from Visakhapatnam and 180 km from Kakinada at 11.30 a.m. on Tuesday, the IMD said. It has come about 50 km closer since 8.30 a.m. and is moving towards the coast at 20 kmph.

About 600 km of railway track in the Vijayawada and Visakhapatnam divisions is under close watch ahead of Cyclone Arnab, Railway Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw said in a post on X on Tuesday. War rooms are working round the clock at the zone, division and Railway Board levels, and senior officials are on site.

Relief wagons with repair material have been placed at Krishna Canal, Bitragunta, Mamidipudi, Visakhapatnam, Palasa and Ponduru. Diesel locomotives, power units and ambulances are on standby at key junctions, and earthmovers and tree cutters are positioned along the route. Wind speed and water levels are being checked every hour, he said.

Nepal has put the country on high alert from Thursday to Saturday. Cyclone Arnab is expected to bring heavy rain, thunderstorms and strong winds there after it crosses the Indian coast, its disaster management authority said. Koshi, Bagmati, Madhesh, Gandaki and Lumbini provinces are likely to be hit hardest on Friday and Saturday.

The high hills and Himalayan areas face a risk of heavy snow, snowstorms and avalanches. Tourists have been told not to travel there during the alert, and those already in these areas to stay in safe places. People living along riverbanks have been warned of possible flooding.

Cyclone Arnab is at its strongest out at sea now. The IMD’s forecast table shows winds of 150 to 160 kmph, gusting to 180 kmph, around midday and evening on Tuesday, while the storm is still over the Bay of Bengal.
It should ease a little before it reaches land close to Yanam early on Wednesday, the winds are forecast at 125-135 kmph, gusting to 150 kmph.
By Wednesday evening its winds should drop below 100 kmph. By Thursday morning it will be a deep depression, and by Friday evening little more than a low-pressure area over central India.

Odisha plans to move at least 48,000 people from low-lying and landslide-prone areas to safety by Tuesday evening, Special Relief Commissioner Rajesh P. Patil told PTI. Gajapati and Nabarangpur districts account for about 11,000 each. The State has readied 135 permanent cyclone shelters and about 1,600 temporary ones, deployed 294 rescue teams and closed schools in eight districts on Tuesday and Wednesday.

Winds of 40 to 50 kmph are likely from Tuesday night, rising to 60 to 70 kmph, gusting to 80 kmph, from early Wednesday in the southern districts of Ganjam, Gajapati, Nabarangpur, Rayagada, Koraput and Malkangiri, the IMD said. It has forecast heavy to very heavy rain of 12 to 20 cm in Puri, Gajapati, Ganjam, Rayagada, Koraput and Malkangiri.

A large tree fell across National Highway 16 on the Tuni-Anakapalli stretch near Regupalan junction in Anakapalli district on Tuesday, blocking traffic. The district police and highway patrol staff cleared it, and vehicles are moving freely again. No one was hurt and no vehicle was damaged.

articles.title: Four new faces join Omar Abdullah’s Cabinet in J&K
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: Jammu and Kashmir Chief Minister Omar Abdullah-led government, on Tuesday (October 27, 2026), inducted four new faces into the Council of Ministers, including an old hand from Srinagar, Ali Muhammad Sagar, and a female face Shameema Firdous, taking the total strength of Cabinet to nine in the Union Territory.

J&K Lieutenant-Governor Manoj Sinha administered the oath of office and secrecy to Mr. Sagar, Ms. Firdous, Mir Saifullah, and Altaf Kaloo at Lok Bhavan in Srinagar. One Minister, Satish Sharma, an Independent candidate from the Jammu province, was dropped from the present Cabinet. Ruling National Conference (NC) ally Congress has decided to stay away “till Statehood is restored”.

#WATCH | Srinagar | Jammu & Kashmir Lieutenant Governor Manoj Sinha administers the oath of office to newly inducted ministers as CM Omar Abdullah expands his Cabinet Mir Saifullah, MLA Trehgam Kupwara, Ali Mohammad Sagar ,MLA Khanyar Srinagar, Shameem Firdous, MLA Habba Kadal Srinagar and Altaf Ahmad Wan, MLA Pahalgam inducted as ministers

Mr. Sagar (68), who represents the Khanyar constituency, is an old hand in the NC and has served as a Minister in the past too. Mr. Sagar and his son Salman Sagar, managed to win two seats from Srinagar district in the 2024 elections.

Ms. Firdous, who represents Srinagar’s Habba Kadal constituency, is the second female Minister in the Cabinet after Sakina Itoo from south Kashmir’s Kulgam. The NC won seven out of eight seats from Srinagar district in the 2024 Assembly elections.
The induction of Mr. Kaloo gives additional representation to south Kashmir, while Mr. Saifullah adds to the representation of north Kashmir, a stronghold of the party.

Under Section 53 of the Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Act, 2019, the Council of Ministers in the UT cannot exceed 10% of the 90-member Assembly. For the past two years, CM Abdullah had only five Ministers in the Cabinet.

articles.title: Omar Abdullah brings Statehood resolution in J&K Assembly amid loud protests by BJP MLAs
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: Jammu and Kashmir Chief Minister Omar Abdullah on Friday moved a resolution on the restoration of Statehood “in continuation of the 2000 autonomy resolution” and evoked protests from the Opposition BJP legislators, who tore the resolution, climbed the tables and opposed any move to discuss autonomy or Article 370 in the Assembly.

“In addition to the Resolutions passed by this House on 26th June 2000 and 6th November 2024, this House calls upon the Government of India for the immediate and urgent restoration of full Statehood to Jammu and Kashmir and resolves that this Resolution be forwarded to Government of India,” reads the resolution moved by Mr. Abdullah in the Supplementary List of Business.

articles.title: What the new E100 vehicle rules mean | Explained
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: The story so far: The Ministry of Road Transport and Highways has amended the Central Motor Vehicles Rules, 1989 , to permit the use of ethanol-based fuels containing up to 100% ethanol (E100) in vehicles. The move paves the way for flex-fuel vehicles, which can run on petrol, ethanol blends of varying proportions, or pure ethanol.
The amendments modify Rule 115, which deals with emission standards and related requirements for motor vehicles, and Rule 115E, which contains additional provisions relating to emission testing.

One of the key changes is the inclusion of E100, or fuel comprising 100% ethanol, alongside E85 in several tables under Rule 115. E85 is a fuel containing up to 85% ethanol, while E100 consists entirely of ethanol, subject to applicable fuel specifications.
The amendments include an explanatory note stating that E85 or E100 may be used only in flex-fuel vehicles designed by original equipment manufacturers.

No. In a press statement, the Ministry sought to allay concerns among motorists, clarifying that a vehicle’s compatibility with E10 or E20 does not establish its suitability for E85. The notification does not require owners of existing vehicles to switch to E85 or modify their vehicles, either now or in the future.

Motorists should check the fuel-compatibility sticker on their vehicle and follow the manufacturer’s guidance in the owner’s manual when choosing fuel at a filling station, the Ministry statement added.

The amendments are expected to facilitate homologation, the official certification process through which authorised agencies, such as the Automotive Research Association of India, verify that vehicles and components comply with technical, safety and environmental standards before they can be approved for sale or use on public roads.
This will help secure type approvals for E100-powered vehicles, supporting their rollout and wider consumer adoption.
Corrections have also been incorporated into fuel classifications, including a reference to gasoline blended with 20% ethanol, or E20, in place of an earlier notation referring to E10.

India achieved its 20% ethanol-blending (E20) target in 2025 , five years ahead of the original 2030 deadline set under the National Policy on Biofuels, 2018. From April 2026, all Bharat Stage-VI (BS-VI) vehicles are required to fully meet E20 emission standards, and all petrol sold across India is mandated to contain 20% ethanol (E20). The policy focus is now widening beyond E20: the government has enabled the regulatory pathway for E85 and E100 vehicles, though these fuels will require compatible flex-fuel vehicles and dedicated dispensing infrastructure.

The main concern is vehicle compatibility. Owners of older or non-E20-compliant vehicles question whether E20 could damage components, raise maintenance costs, or leave them without access to lower-ethanol petrol.

Consumers also question E20’s effect on fuel economy. Ethanol has a lower energy density than petrol; while the government estimates a 5% decline in mileage, some consumers say the loss is greater. Dealers, meanwhile, warn that ethanol’s affinity for water could raise contamination risks during the monsoon, strengthening the case for separate storage and dispensing systems for higher blends. These concerns have prompted calls for a transparent assessment.

articles.title: BPCL shifts crude sourcing towards Middle East as Russian oil loses price edge
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: Bharat Petroleum Corporation Ltd (BPCL) tapped more into Middle Eastern crude as Russian oil lost its price advantage and also due to rising freight costs, with the shift becoming more pronounced in November, Vetsa Ramakrishna Gupta, Director (Finance), told analysts during a post-results call on Monday.

“Our spot crude share remained at around 67% in the second quarter, while Russian grade accounted for approximately 37% of our total crude procurement, both broadly in line with the previous quarter,” Mr. Gupta said, adding that the company increased purchases from the Middle East as supplies from the region improved.

Russia accounted for 37% of BPCL’s crude basket in the September quarter, followed by Saudi Arabia at 19%, Abu Dhabi at 17%, the U.S. at 9% and Oman at 6%. The remaining supplies came from countries contributing 1-4% each.
As of September-end, BPCL held about 22 days of crude inventory, with sourcing requirements tied up through December.
Mr. Gupta said the share of Russian crude in October was expected to remain “more or less the same”, although procurement volumes would be lower for November.

“October, our requirement from Russia slightly came down but in the month of November, the cargoes from Russia significantly reduced due to [reduced] commercial viability [compared to that from Middle East], mainly the increase in the freight,” he said, adding that the company did not receive attractive offers for Russian crude in November.

Russian crude was available at a premium of $12-$13 per barrel over benchmark prices in October. The premium has narrowed to $1-$2 per barrel for December cargoes, Mr. Gupta said, although freight costs remain high.
“Maybe today, Russian cargo is preferable than a Middle Eastern cargo for December month because November [procurement] we have already concluded,” he said.

BPCL also diversified its liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) sourcing during the quarter. Supplies from the Arab Gulf improved, while the US accounted for about 48% of LPG imports in the September quarter.
Softening Saudi Contract Prices (Saudi CP), the benchmark for LPG pricing, helped reduce under-recoveries to an average ₹290 per cylinder in the September quarter from ₹507 in the June quarter.

Under-recoveries are expected to be ₹245 per cylinder in October and are expected to rise to ₹328 in November, Mr. Gupta said. BPCL currently holds 32 days of LPG inventory, including supplies in transit.
The company has also diversified liquefied natural gas (LNG) procurement by increasing spot purchases from the US, Oman and West Africa.

articles.title: UPI and the cost of policy reversal
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: The government has just given itself the legal room to tax the very payment habit it spent a decade building. Tucked into the Taxation and Other Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026, is an amendment to Section 10A of the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007, which would allow the government to notify charges on specified electronic payment modes. The number being proposed is a Merchant Discount Rate (MDR) of 0.25–0.5% on UPI transactions above ₹2,000. The official stand is that this threshold would touch only about five per cent of transactions by volume, sparing the milk-and-vegetable payments that make up the bulk of UPI’s use. But it would cover roughly 65% of transaction value, which is precisely why it matters.
This is not a small, technical fix. It runs counter to a decade-long policy commitment and deserves more scrutiny than it has received.

Consider the arc. Demonetisation in November 2016 was justified, among other things, as a push towards a less-cash economy. UPI, launched earlier that year, became the vehicle for that push, and its zero-MDR regime was a deliberate subsidy to get merchants and consumers off cash. It worked spectacularly. UPI now processes more transactions each month than most of the world’s card networks combined. Having successfully weaned the country away from cash and towards electronic payments, the government now wants to undercut the very success it engineered.

There seems to be a continued pattern of privileging one payment mode over others via policy. India has long taxed even credit cards. Credit card interest and fees attract 18% GST, making the use of credit cards unnecessarily costly. Taxing interest on revolving credit is unusual by international standards; most jurisdictions treat consumer credit interest as a private financial cost, not a taxable service. India taxes it as if using a credit card itself is a luxury.

Now UPI, the payment rail the government spent political capital promoting, is in line for similar treatment. The pattern suggests a need for a more coherent payments policy than giving in to the temptation to tax every transaction that can be observed.
There are at least two problems with this specific move beyond the optics.

First, basic economic theory tells us that the person on whom a tax is levied and the person who actually bears its cost are not always the same. Moreover, UPI or any payments interface is a two-sided market, and taxing two-sided markets is genuinely tricky.

The MDR would nominally fall on merchants, as argued by the government, collected via banks and the National Payments Corporation of India’s ecosystem. But whether that cost gets passed through to merchants, on to consumers, or absorbed by banks and payment service providers depends on competitive intensity on each side of the market. Banks and fintechs compete for merchant relationships and cannot easily raise prices without losing volume to a rival offering free UPI acceptance.

The more likely outcome is that intermediaries — the banks and PSPs that built and maintain the plumbing — absorb the cost, which erodes their incentive to invest in reliability, fraud prevention and expansion into underserved segments. A tax that cannot be reliably passed through does not disappear; it most likely shows up later as degraded service or slower innovation. This is completely counterintuitive if government is proposing this tax as necessary to fund the next stage of UPI growth.

Second, UPI has done real work on financial inclusion at the margin. It has pulled informal transactions into a recorded, traceable digital trail — the very outcome that formalisation and tax-compliance advocates have wanted for years. There have also been attempts to provide credit based on the digital trail created by electronic payments. Every rupee that moves through UPI instead of cash is a rupee the financial institutions can eventually see and use to build a spending profile.

Charging the rail directly could undercut the incentive to use it, cutting against long-standing financial inclusion goals. The government does not need to raise revenue from every rupee that moves electronically; it needs those rupees to keep moving electronically, because that is what delivers the inclusion and compliance dividends it has been chasing since 2016.

Ideally, which payment mode to adopt should be an economic decision for participating actors. Factors such as the size of the business, consumer preferences, and relative cost of using alternative payment systems should determine their usage. Deliberate policy intervention and the current government’s war on cash tilted the scales in favour of UPI. Taxing it now — however nominal or small — could change its usage patterns, and policymakers should not be surprised if one outcome is reduced UPI usage.

articles.title: How India’s life insurance sector funds government expenditure
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: When the government borrows, the question that follows is rarely asked aloud: who lends? A large part of the answer is the life insurance sector. Every year, millions of households across India pay premiums into life insurance policies. That money is reinvested, for decades, in the very securities that finance government expenditure — roads, railways, water supplies, hospitals, defence. The household protecting itself against the loss of its breadwinner is simultaneously, and unknowingly, lending to the sovereign [the Central government]. Life insurers collectively hold close to a quarter of India’s outstanding central government dated securities, based on RBI and IRDAI data — a share that has remained stable even as the total sovereign debt stock expanded by around 40 per cent in three years. This is not a number that appears in budget speeches or parliamentary debates. It is, however, a number that matters.

The stoic and resilient quality of the sector’s sovereign support is as significant as its scale. Life insurers write policies with tenures of twenty, thirty, sometimes forty years. Government securities are the natural habitat of long-duration liabilities — the only asset class that absorbs this scale of funds at matching tenures without distorting the market. Unlike foreign portfolio investors, whose appetite fluctuates with global risk sentiment, insurance companies buy and hold. They do not exit when oil prices rise or when a geopolitical event triggers a reassessment of emerging market exposure. Their participation is counter-cyclical by design — stable precisely when other buyers become unreliable. A steady domestic base of long-horizon holders reduces rollover risk and moderates borrowing costs across the maturity spectrum.
Life insurers buy when others sell, hold when others exit, and reinvest when others pause. That is the structural consequence of writing long-duration promises to millions of policyholders.

The sector’s contribution is not evenly distributed. The Life Insurance Corporation of India carries the dominant share — a consequence of its scale, its predominantly participating product mix, and the duration of its in-force book. Its March 2025 regulatory filing with IRDAI (Form L-26) confirms that sovereign paper accounts for nearly 63 per cent of its non-linked policyholder corpus — well above the regulatory minimum, and a direct expression of what long-duration liabilities demand at scale.

LIC holds approximately 19 per cent of all outstanding central government dated securities — a figure confirmed by the RBI’s Public Debt Management Quarterly Report for FY24, the most recently published data. LIC’s IRDAI regulatory filings for March 2025 give the institutional reality in absolute terms: ₹20.2 lakh crore in central government securities alone, and ₹32.3 lakh crore in total government and government-guaranteed securities across all funds. These are not estimates. They are figures LIC files with its regulator every quarter and that any researcher can access on the IRDAI website. This makes LIC the single largest institutional holder of Indian government’s debt.
Government securities are the natural habitat of long-duration liabilities — the only asset class that absorbs this scale of funds at matching tenures without distorting the market.

Private life insurers, with a higher proportion of unit-linked and shorter-tenure products, contribute a smaller fraction today. As they grow and deepen their traditional offerings, their sovereign allocations will follow the same structural logic.

The regulator has already recognised the systemic dimension of this function: IRDAI designates LIC as a Domestic Systemically Important Insurer every year, describing it as an institution whose distress would cause significant dislocation in the financial system. That designation, rightly made on insurance-sector grounds, points toward a wider truth — the dislocation would extend into the sovereign borrowing programme itself.

Insurers in Japan, the United Kingdom, and South Korea are among the largest holders of their respective governments’ long-dated securities, not because regulation mandates it but because their liability profiles demand it. India’s life insurance sector is following the same path.

India’s life insurance penetration stood at 2.7 per cent of GDP in FY25, the third consecutive year of decline from a pandemic-era peak of 3.2 per cent, against a global life average of 3.0 per cent. Three regulatory interventions between 2023 and 2024 — restructured distribution economics, taxation on certain high-value policies, and mandatory product repricing, simultaneously, has compressed new businesses. While each was defensible in isolation, their cumulative effect was adverse. The sector is recovering. But the episode illustrates a risk worth noting: when multiple regulatory actions compress new business at once, the household savings that would otherwise have flowed into the sovereign debt market through insurance, reduce or find shorter-duration homes elsewhere. The sovereign borrowing programme may not notice this in the short term. Over a decade, it would.
Banking commands policy attention in proportion to its systemic importance. Insurance, which quietly holds close to a quarter of outstanding central government dated securities, does not.

The case for deeper insurance penetration is most often made in the language of household financial protection — the uninsured family, the inadequate sum assured, a mis-sold product or an unsettled claim. These are legitimate concerns. But there is a parallel case, made in the language of sovereign fiscal stability, that has not been fully articulated in public policy discourse. If the reliability of India’s domestic sovereign funding base is a macroeconomic priority given the scale of annual borrowing requirements, then the depth and health of the life insurance sector remain directly relevant to that priority.

articles.title: Swiping in dark: The hidden cost of plastic money
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: A smartwatch bought on impulse, a costly phone ordered just for the thrill of owning it, a festive sale too tempting to resist. In isolation, each swipe may seem harmless, yet the danger lies in accumulation. Money spent in moments of desire can quietly turn into a burden that outlasts the fleeting gratification. Small indulgences, if they add up to a sizeable bill, can take a toll on the monthly budget and derail carefully planned financial goals.
The litmus test comes knocking much later, after the swipes have ended: a shocking bill. Now, to overcome the shock, cardholders often look for a shortcut: paying just the minimum due.

The minimum-due loop is one of the most deceptive traps of a credit card. Paying only this negligible fraction may help avert immediate late-payment penalties and default notices. However, it allows the bulk of your debt to linger and compound.

Crucially, carrying a due attracts interest and simultaneously revokes the interest-free grace period for subsequent purchases. Any new spend begins accruing interest charges immediately at typical annual rates of 36% to 42%, compounded monthly, until the entire bill is cleared in full. If the minimum-due route is a slow leak, ignoring the bill payment entirely is an outright rupture. Failing to pay the minimum due carries far more severe consequences.

The bank would immediately flag the account as overdue, levying hefty late-payment penalties on top of the standard charges. If the default crosses a stipulated time, the bank reports the delinquency to CIBIL and other credit bureaus, leaving a long-lasting scar on your score.

When the bill is bulky, cardholders often lean towards another tempting escape hatch: easy EMIs. Converting a purchase into equated monthly instalments does not erase the cost; rather, it locks you into a high-margin contract.
You forfeit the upfront discounts that are often bundled with full payment, while a relentless 18% GST is slapped onto the interest portion of every single EMI.
By splitting past impulse purchases across future months, you silently mortgage your upcoming cash flows. The bitter truth: the thrill of owning fades fast, but the bill of burden goes on and on.

Paying your bill on time is only half the battle. Even if you are punctual in clearing the bills, it’s not a total financial hygiene. When the usage on your card is close to its ceiling, you trigger an alarm button inside credit bureaus. Lenders gauge your financial stability through credit utilisation, and crossing the 30% threshold paints a picture of being cash hungry. Even if you do not default payment, a high usage of credit erodes your CIBIL score rating, transforming routine swipes into a hidden roadblock when you eventually apply for a home or vehicle loan.
Gliding your credit card smoothly into an ATM for quick cash would force you to endure a rough patch with huge money leaks.

On most credit cards, cash withdrawals carry zero grace period, meaning standard interest rates of 36 to 42% begin compounding moments after the currency is dispensed. Even on select promotional cards that tout an interest-free window, the fixed fees bite hard.

For instance, banks usually cap single ATM withdrawals at ₹10,000 while levying a flat processing fee of around ₹199 plus GST on every single attempt. Therefore, a requirement of ₹50,000 forces you to glide into the vending tunnel five times, instantly draining roughly over ₹1,000 in raw processing charges alone.

articles.title: Ethanol tender sparks feedstock concerns as rice gains ground over maize
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: The Oil Marketing Companies’ (OMCs) latest ethanol procurement tender for Ethanol Supply Year (ESY) 2026–27 has triggered concerns among grain-based ethanol producers and sections of the sugar industry over feedstock pricing, allocation priorities and the potential implications for the sector.

The tender sets procurement prices at ₹60.32 a litre for surplus foodgrains (SFG), with a stated cap of 108 crore litres for the first three quarters; ₹64 a litre for damaged foodgrains (DFG); and ₹66 a litre for maize, plus an additional ₹2.79 a litre. While ethanol produced from sugarcane juice, sugar syrup and B-heavy molasses has been excluded, C-heavy molasses-based ethanol remains eligible for procurement.

The Grain Ethanol Manufacturers Association (GEMA) has argued that the tender places a disproportionate burden on rice-based feedstocks, particularly SFG and DFG, while potentially weakening maize’s role as an industrial feedstock.
The pricing differential has also created uncertainty over how procurement demand will be distributed among the different feedstock categories.

According to industry estimates, DFG-based ethanol allocation during ESY 2025–26 was approximately 60 crore litres. For ESY 2026–27, the industry anticipates that the allocation could exceed 700 crore litres.

C.K. Jain, president of GEMA, said a balanced ethanol policy must support viable production from both maize and rice, with procurement prices reflecting their different cost structures and allocations providing reasonable visibility to producers. He added that the government and OMCs should review the pricing and allocation framework.

GEMA has also questioned whether maize will receive adequate procurement opportunities under the lowest-price-based allocation mechanism. It has called for greater clarity on the methodology for feedstock-wise allocation and the role envisaged for maize in meeting the country’s ethanol requirements.

The Indian Sugar & Bio-Energy Manufacturers Association (ISMA) has welcomed the exclusion of ethanol produced from sugarcane juice, sugar syrup and B-heavy molasses, arguing that the approach is consistent with the need to safeguard domestic sugar availability amid uncertainty over the forthcoming crop.
C-heavy molasses-based ethanol, it noted, allows sugar mills to continue contributing to the ethanol-blending programme without diverting recoverable sugar.
However, ISMA has raised concerns over the preferential allocation granted to dedicated ethanol plants holding Long-Term Offtake Agreements under the ESY 2026–27 tender.
While the provision is already in place for the current year, its continuation in subsequent years could hurt the sugar industry, the association said.

articles.title: Mbappe dropped by Chinese brands for ‘offending national sentiments’
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Foreign Visits & UN/G20/BRICS
fullParagraphs: Kylian Mbappe was dropped on Tuesday (October 27, 2026) by two major brands in China after a video circulated online in which the French football superstar apparently joked about former leader Mao Zedong.
In China jokes about Mao, the country’s founding leader who died in 1976, are considered disrespectful and remain a social taboo.

“Our company firmly opposes and has a zero-tolerance policy towards any behaviour that offends national sentiments,” drinks giant Dongpeng said in a statement, adding that “with immediate effect we are terminating all cooperation with Kylian Mbappe”.
Adverts showing AI-generated images of the 27-year-old France captain drinking a Dongpeng sports drink were regularly shown in China during this year’s World Cup.
Mengniu, China’s largest dairy producer, also cut ties with the Real Madrid forward, who until this incident was hugely popular among Chinese fans with millions of followers on social media.
Mbappe is fondly nicknamed “Guigui”, the Chinese translation of “Turtle”, due to his popularity as a character in a Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles meme.
“With immediate effect our company is terminating all cooperation with Kylian Mbappe,” Mengniu said in a statement.
“Mengniu firmly opposes and has a zero-tolerance policy towards any words or actions that hurt the feelings of the Chinese people,” it added.

The announcements came after a video emerged online with Mbappe saying that the funniest internet meme he had seen was of his face photo-shopped onto that of “some guy — I think he’s a Chinese dictator”.
This was an apparent reference to a meme of Mbappe superimposed on an image of Mao, one of several using the footballer’s face and other historical figures.
The authenticity of the video could not immediately be verified by AFP Fact Check.
“Dongpeng Beverage ends cooperation with Mbappe” was the top-trending topic on Chinese social media site Weibo.

articles.title: New UNSC permanent members without veto would be 'second-class': India
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Foreign Visits & UN/G20/BRICS
fullParagraphs: India has asserted that any reform of the UN Security Council that creates a new category of permanent members without veto powers would effectively relegate them to “second-class” status, leaving the existing five permanent powers in control of the decision-making process.

China, France, Russia, the U.K. and the U.S. are the five permanent members of the 15-member Security Council and enjoy veto powers. The Council also has 10 non-permanent members elected for two-year terms.

India's Permanent Representative to the UN, Ambassador Harish Parvathaneni, on Monday (October 26, 2026) said the veto must be held by all permanent members of a reformed Council as long as the provision exists, stressing that fairness and justice demand equal rights and responsibilities for all permanent members.
"India's position on the veto is principled and well known... We reiterate that as long as the veto exists, it must be held by all permanent members of a reformed Council," he said.

Addressing the Inter-Governmental (IGN) plenary on 'Cluster Debate on the Question of the Veto' in the UN General Assembly, Parvathaneni said a reform that expands the Security Council by "creating another category of long-term members without the veto effectively makes them 'second-class' members and would not change the decision-making dynamic of the P5".

Creating a new category of permanent members, with or without veto powers, would further complicate an already difficult discussion and "entrench the very inequity we are seeking to correct", he said.
"Periodic elections and the concept of permanency are fundamentally contradictory,” the diplomat said.

“History has a lesson for us,” he said, recalling that the only expansion of the Security Council, in 1965, increased the number of non-permanent members from six to 10 while retaining five permanent members.
The ratio of permanent to elected members shifted from 5:6 to 5:10, further strengthening the relative power of the P5, Mr. Parvathaneni said.

India has consistently called for expanding both the permanent and non-permanent categories of membership, warning that reform efforts would border on "failure" if they focused solely on increasing the number of non-permanent members.

New Delhi has been at the forefront of years-long efforts to achieve reform of the Security Council, saying the body, founded in 1945, is not fit for purpose in the 21st century and does not reflect contemporary geopolitical realities.
India has consistently underscored that it rightly deserves a permanent seat at the horse-shoe table.

articles.title: Netanyahu, wanted by ICC, battles for political survival as Israel goes to the polls
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Foreign Visits & UN/G20/BRICS
fullParagraphs: Thousands took to the streets of Tel Aviv on Saturday (October 24, 2026), demanding accountability for the failure to prevent the October 7, 2023 Hamas attack. The anti-government demonstration came just three days ahead of what is being described as one of Israel’s most consequential elections.
The protest adds to the pressure on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, whose bid to retain power comes amid mounting criticism of his government’s handling of domestic and international issues.

For most of Mr. Netanyahu’s latest term, Israel has been embroiled in one conflict or the other. In less than a year of him taking the seat as Prime Minister in 2022, Israel witnessed the Hamas attack in which more than 1,200 were killed, and about 250 were taken hostage. This stirred concerns and protests over security failure and hostage releases.
Mr. Netanyahu then promised a “total victory” over Hamas and other enemies.

Three years later, the war is still dragging on inconclusively. What began as Israel’s response to the Hamas attack spiralled into an all-out regional conflict in West Asia, with the country launching attacks in Gaza, Iran, Lebanon, Yemen, and Syria.
His involvement of the U.S. in its war against Iran on February 28 has impacted countries much beyond West Asia, as it disrupted global energy supply.

He has also intensified Israel’s operations in the West Bank and has increased settlement projects in the region. This has not only severely impacted his ratings as a Prime Minister but has also isolated Israel internationally.

According to a Pew Research Centre survey conducted earlier this year, majorities in more than thirty surveyed countries expressed unfavourable views of Israel and little or no confidence in Mr. Netanyahu. Even within Israel, the military actions have not alleviated the security concerns. A survey by the Israel Democracy Institute in July this year showed that only a little over one-third of Israelis think that the security situation is better than what it was before ‘Operation Roaring Lion’. The constant state of conflict has also come at severe domestic costs— high inflation, a high cost of living, longer and more exhausting service for Army personnel, a soaring national debt, and declining business investment.
Further, he has been accused of weakening the judiciary and endangering democracy with his far-right government.
For Mr. Netanyahu, the longest-serving Prime Minister seeking the seventh term, a lot is at stake personally too.

According to Arik Rudnitzky, from the Israel Democracy Institute in Jerusalem, these elections are the most decisive political test for Mr. Netanyahu as the leader of the Likud Party. He told The Hindu : “I believe these elections are crucial to the political future of Netanyahu. If he no longer serves as Prime Minister, then he has to face his legal issues, and especially the file is being handled right now in court, with the accusations that he has to defend himself.”

The corruption trial, which began in 2020, has been under way for six years now. Mr. Netanyahu has been indicted on charges of bribery, fraud, and breach of trust. He has, however, denied these charges, and the case continues in court. Without the political power, reports suggest that Mr. Netanyahu would have fewer chances of gaining immunity or reasons to postpone hearings.

articles.title: U.S. judge halts tree-cutting at Trump’s golf course project
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Foreign Visits & UN/G20/BRICS
fullParagraphs: A U.S. federal judge ruled on Monday (October 26, 2026) to halt tree-cutting at a public golf course in the heart of the capital, after hundreds of trees were felled in Donald Trump's pet project.

An avid golfer who owns courses around the world, the U.S. President has called for Washington's East Potomac Golf Links, a public course with affordable rates, to be remodelled into a facility capable of hosting major championship-calibre events.

The early demolition for the overhaul had charged ahead despite an environmental group's lawsuit, and opposition from local golfers who argue the 100-year-old course is a rare spot where they can affordably play the sport.

"The Court ENJOINS defendants from removing or damaging additional trees on East Potomac Golf Course and ORDERS them to provide ten business days' written advance notice before making any irreparable modification to any forms or features of East Potomac Park, pending the outcome of this litigation," District Judge Ana Reyes wrote in Monday's 70-page order.

"The Government felled hundreds of trees from the East Potomac Golf Course without real notice, even though it knew of the scheduled removal at least a week prior," Ms. Reyes said, adding that they were "healthy, nonhazardous trees."

Mr. Trump said this month that construction was set to start in November on the 18-hole course. He insisted on Monday that the site would close for renovation as scheduled, on November 15, and pledged to appeal Ms. Reyes' decision.
"The judge has absolutely no right to hold up this very important and beautiful Project," Mr. Trump wrote on Truth Social.
More than 500 trees have already been cut down, the judge wrote.
The court "does not speak for the trees," Ms. Reyes wrote in her order, in reference to the Dr. Seuss book The Lorax.

articles.title: Microsoft offers voluntary exit packages to 60,000 staff, with some Indian teams eligible
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Foreign Visits & UN/G20/BRICS
fullParagraphs: Microsoft is offering voluntary buyouts to about 60,000 employees, the company said on Monday (October 26, 2026), roughly a quarter of its workforce, as the tech giant seeks to cut costs while pouring money into artificial intelligence.

Staff on select teams in the United States, Canada, India and Britain at vice-president level and below will be eligible, a Microsoft spokesperson said, while some groups of employees, including some working on data centres, sales and marketing, are excluded.

“The Voluntary Exit Offer reflects an important part of how we’re evolving our approach to change: creating greater flexibility and, where possible, more ways for employees to shape their next chapter,” Amy Coleman, an executive vice-president and chief people officer, told employees in a memo.
It’s the second voluntary buyout offer that Microsoft has offered employees this year.
In April, the company reportedly offered around seven percent of its U.S. workforce the option to retire early.
Around 30% of those eligible took the voluntary retirement plan, according to CNBC .
Microsoft had 2,23,000 employees globally at the end of June, down from 2,28,000 at the end of 2025, according to regulatory filings.
Around 27% of Microsoft’s workforce is eligible for the new buyout offer.
The company is expected to report quarterly earnings later this week.
As major tech giants continue to spend heavily on AI-related investments, concerns persist about the impact of the technology on jobs.
Even industry insiders, such as Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, have warned of mass job losses.
Netflix will reportedly cut around 6% of its workforce, or 1,000 jobs, U.S. media reported last week.

articles.title: Why scratching an itch feel so good
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Updates, Tech & Climate Reports
fullParagraphs: As it turns out, scientists have wondered about this too. There is even a research paper titled “The Pleasurability of Scratching an Itch”. Yes, you read that right. So, what exactly is going on between your skin, nerves and brain when you scratch? Let’s find out.

Seems like a weird question? Well, science turns every weird question into a curious one. That is why, an itch is more than just an annoying feeling on your skin. It is a signal from your body telling you that something may be irritating it. Specialised nerve cells in your skin detect the irritation and send signals through your nerves to your spinal cord and brain. Your brain then registers the sensation as an itch — and that is when you get the urge to scratch.
When you scratch an itchy spot, the action activates pain-sensing nerves in your skin. These signals travel to the spinal cord and brain and can temporarily suppress the itch signals.

But there is another player: serotonin. Scratching can cause the release of serotonin in the spinal cord. While serotonin is often associated with feelings such as happiness and well-being, in this case it can also affect how the brain processes itch and pain. It helps dampen the itch for a while, giving you that satisfying feeling of relief.
The catch? Serotonin can also activate certain itch-related nerve cells, which may explain why the relief from scratching is temporary — and why you may soon want to scratch again.

So, why does scratching feel not just relieving, but actually good? Part of the answer lies in the brain’s response to the sensation. Scratching provides a strong physical sensation that competes with the itch, while the sudden drop in discomfort brings a feeling of relief.

That contrast, going from “ugh, this is itchy” to “ahh, finally!” can make scratching feel surprisingly satisfying. In other words, your brain is not only noticing the scratch; it is also enjoying the relief that follows.

That satisfying scratch can come with a downside. Scratching too much can damage the skin, cause inflammation and even lead to small cuts that allow bacteria to enter. In some cases, the irritation can make the itching worse — giving you another reason to scratch.
Apparently, yes. In the study, researchers induced an itch at three different spots — the forearm, ankle and back — and then measured how intense the itch felt and how pleasurable scratching was.

The ankle and back produced stronger itch sensations than the forearm. Interestingly, scratching was also rated as more pleasurable at these two sites. On the back, scratching was particularly effective at reducing the itch.

The researchers also found that the stronger the itch, the greater the pleasure from scratching at the forearm and ankle. So, when an itch is really bothering you, finally hitting the right spot may feel even more satisfying.

articles.title: Into the “brain rot” psyche
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Updates, Tech & Climate Reports
fullParagraphs: Here, feed it this reel. And another one. This one’s just a cat doing a dance challenge. Simply harmless. Yes, harmless. Like it to get more.
Time pass? Boredom? The all-knowing algorithm will take care of it. Keep liking. Don’t stop.
Reality is too complex. No words to describe it? Watch this reel. More and some more. The brain is quiet.

Researchers, scientists and doctors alike have always fussed over the brain, psychologically and medically. Contemporary internet culture gives them another reason to do it — brain rot. It was named the Oxford Word of the Year in 2024 . Surely, we have heard all about it.

Brain rot’s public fame from the confines of social media brought to light several serious concerns regarding the effects of present-day social media use patterns on the brain, typically among the younger generation who relatively have an upperhand when it comes to grasping and using digital tech.
Illustration by Esra Eslen. | Photo Credit: Wikimedia Commons

Doomscrolling, low attention span, feedback loop, instant gratification, too much screen time, overstimulation, memory disruption, etc. stand out as aspects fuelling a collective brain rot. As the word suggests, the idea is one of rotting — rotting of the high intelligence and cognition that puts humans on the top among the creatures of Earth. How interestingly ironic it is, this concept, culturally perceiving that the same intelligence that created all this brilliant tech is mediating the ‘rotting’.

Let’s put aside the negative connotations and start with a clean plate. Initially, brain rot’s popularity had brought immense panic among the adults. It was a threat and some even viewed it as a sort of “Gen-Z disease”. The thing is, brain rot is somewhere between a pop label and mental malady which means arguments on and around the concept are continuously being shaped and reshaped. The behaviours and effects are still being monitored.

Interestingly, some brain science and psychology studies this year have described brainrot as participatory, allaying the particularly gloomy theme that it is a downgrading cognitive characteristic of an entire generation of teenagers. These studies highlight two important things about the psyche of brainrot — how we use our free time and participation. It challenges the notion of brain rot as a helpless passive setup that affects all youth. The baton is in our hands. Let’s analyse this again.

When do we use social media mostly? During free time. Now, in my free time, if I like a short reel video and more videos like that pop up on my feed, I’m the participant participating in the algorithm, aren’t I? A 2026 study by Emilie Owens published in the journal New Media & Society revealed that brain rot can be understood as “decompression-driven” and that teenagers are “actively resisting” productivity similar to how people binge-watch or even play games. Huh, very interesting. Imagine I’m home after work and my brain is filled with thoughts related to work. I need my brain to shut up, so I open social media for quick distraction and relaxation. If it were years back, after coming from school, I would likely go out to play instead. If a 40-something guy started using social media right now and drove the algorithm to keep giving him all these new varieties of low-quality and unchallenging reels, isn’t he also a citizen of the brainrot kingdom?

Chaithanya N C, a neuropsychologist at the Ananthapuri Hospital and Research Institute, pointed out the larger case — “it is not that teenagers are at fault, rather, the digital environment is set up that way and in this case, demanding such ultra-short, nonsensical videos to grab their attention.” Owens notes that binge-watching has an end point, i.e. when the show ends, whereas scrolling is infinite. The social media algorithmic bias driven by feedback loops (user interactions are taken as triggers which shape the future content) point to a need that the person using the social media has to have a greater awareness and control of the information they get.

Chaithanya says, “AI in itself is not strictly causative of brain rot, but the type of content consumed and the need for engagement may be associated with brain rot. AI tools make it easier to generate large amounts of repetitive, absurd, or low-quality content that can induce mental states of brain rot, which include fragmented attention, a need for constant stimulation to escape boredom and doomscrolling.”

articles.title: What is ‘human composting’ — how does it work?
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Updates, Tech & Climate Reports
fullParagraphs: What should happen to your body after you die? It’s hardly a topic you’d bring up over dinner, but it’s a decision that will eventually need to be made, either by you or by those you leave behind.

In Australia, the choice has traditionally been between burial and cremation. However, concerns about environmental impact, limited cemetery space and the desire for more sustainable alternatives have encouraged interest in other approaches.
These include natural burial, water cremation and shrouded cremation — where no coffin is used.

Now, New South Wales has become the first Australian state to pass legislation allowing another option: “human composting”, technically known as natural organic reduction, and legally termed “terramation”. The process uses microorganisms to transform human remains into a compost-like material.
📢 So-called terramation will become legal in NSW, with several MPs revealing they want their own bodies turned into soil after they die. [image or embed]
The idea of turning a human body into compost might sound unusual, or even unsettling. But how does it actually work? Is it a better alternative to existing methods?
To answer these questions, we first need to understand decomposition and its essential role in nature.
Throughout history, humans have developed rituals to protect, preserve and dress the dead. Some want a quick return to the earth, while others seek to preserve the body.
From ancient burial vessels and elaborate tombs to coffins, shrouds and embalming, these practices reflect cultural and religious beliefs. They also affect how bodies decompose.
Decomposition begins shortly after death. As cells break down, microorganisms already living inside the body, along with those from the surrounding environment, begin breaking down its tissues.

Carrion insects, particularly flies and beetles, can feed on soft tissues remarkably quickly when temperature, moisture and access to the body are favourable. This is nature’s way of recycling organic matter and returning nutrients to the environment.
The body does not simply disappear. But the timescale and extent of its transformation depend on the conditions, processes and materials involved.

articles.title: Microsoft offers voluntary exit packages to 60,000 staff, with some Indian teams eligible
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Updates, Tech & Climate Reports
fullParagraphs: Microsoft is offering voluntary buyouts to about 60,000 employees, the company said on Monday (October 26, 2026), roughly a quarter of its workforce, as the tech giant seeks to cut costs while pouring money into artificial intelligence.

Staff on select teams in the United States, Canada, India and Britain at vice-president level and below will be eligible, a Microsoft spokesperson said, while some groups of employees, including some working on data centres, sales and marketing, are excluded.

“The Voluntary Exit Offer reflects an important part of how we’re evolving our approach to change: creating greater flexibility and, where possible, more ways for employees to shape their next chapter,” Amy Coleman, an executive vice-president and chief people officer, told employees in a memo.
It’s the second voluntary buyout offer that Microsoft has offered employees this year.
In April, the company reportedly offered around seven percent of its U.S. workforce the option to retire early.
Around 30% of those eligible took the voluntary retirement plan, according to CNBC .
Microsoft had 2,23,000 employees globally at the end of June, down from 2,28,000 at the end of 2025, according to regulatory filings.
Around 27% of Microsoft’s workforce is eligible for the new buyout offer.
The company is expected to report quarterly earnings later this week.
As major tech giants continue to spend heavily on AI-related investments, concerns persist about the impact of the technology on jobs.
Even industry insiders, such as Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, have warned of mass job losses.
Netflix will reportedly cut around 6% of its workforce, or 1,000 jobs, U.S. media reported last week.

articles.title: A final surge: On Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s triumph in Brazil
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: At one point, it seemed almost impossible for Brazil’s 80-year-old President, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, to turn the tide after finishing second to Flávio Bolsonaro in the first round of elections on October 4. In Brazil’s history, no candidate who has finished second in the first round has gone on to win the presidential run-off. Most of the candidates who dropped out after the first round were from the right. Flávio’s Liberal Party cemented its position in both houses of Congress, while right-wing candidates won several provincial elections. But Lula, a former trade unionist and organiser, who lost a finger in an accident as a teenager, was not ready to give up. Lula and his Workers’ Party identified campaign weaknesses, shifted their attention to economic issues, promised growth and welfare, and persuaded more voters to turn out for Sunday’s run-off. Lula won 51.7% of the vote against Flávio’s 48.2%, a greater lead than his victory against Jair Bolsonaro, Flavio’s father, four years ago. Over the weeks, Lula turned the right-wing’s gains in the first round against it, highlighting the threats that a Bolsonaro victory could pose to democracy and civil rights. Flávio’s campaign pledge to free his father — he is serving a 27-year prison sentence for attempting to overturn Lula’s 2022 victory, and impeach Supreme Court judges — only heightened the concerns of voters outside the right wing, who rallied behind a familiar face.

Lula unleashed a social media campaign to mobilise younger voters. A WhatsApp channel called ‘Lula’s Army’ with 11 million followers spread his message of continuity. He also announced plans to expand a cash payout scheme for the poor, a new debt relief package and entrepreneur-friendly measures. In the northeast, the Workers’ Party’s stronghold, he gained nearly three million votes and made considerable gains in the working-class neighbourhoods of big cities, including São Paulo. A relatively stable economic record, marked by growth and falling unemployment over the past three and a half years, also lent credibility to Lula’s appeal. His victory bucks the recent trend in South America, where Washington-aligned right-wing and conservative forces have gained ground. While Lula offers predictable stability and social and economic inclusiveness, he could also be, as the President of South America’s largest economy, a voice of resistance to Donald Trump’s imperial ambitions. At the same time, Lula will have to work with a right-wing-controlled Congress to advance his agenda. He should seek to build legislative consensus while focusing on addressing the economic challenges of Brazil, which remains one of the most unequal major world economies.

articles.title: Dubious retreat: On the National Medical Commission and its MSMER
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: The National Medical Commission (NMC) has denotified and withdrawn its 2023 Maintenance of Standards of Medical Education Regulations (MSMER ), diminishing the framework of penalties vis-à-vis educational standards and infrastructure at medical colleges. The move is noteworthy as the MSMER provided for fines of up to ₹5 lakh on faculty members and administrators for submitting false information. Fortunately, the Medical Assessment and Rating Board (MARB) retains the power to fine errant institutions up to ₹1 crore under the 2023 Establishment of Medical Institutions, Assessment and Rating Regulations . MSMER was lauded for its intention to crack down on the deep-seated corruption and malpractice in medical colleges, particularly over ‘ghost faculty’ and ‘ghost patients’. The NMC’s justification is that MSMER also introduced a parallel mechanism allowing undergraduate and postgraduate boards to evaluate institutions, stepping on the MARB’s toes. However, why the NMC scrapped MSMER wholesale is unclear. The 2023 Postgraduate Medical Education Regulations remain in force and include a provision to fine individual faculty members at postgraduate medical colleges. Non-compliance among medical colleges is not uncommon and seldom nipped in the bud, even as the number of medical seats swells while the transparency of the medical education system has not improved.

Notwithstanding the provision to fine individuals at postgraduate centres, the MARB and the NMC can only penalise institutions, which is harder and risks creating a perverse incentive to accommodate rather than punish, and could mitigate the fear that keeps administrators honest. MSMER also specified timelines to appeal penalties. Although the MARB regulations retain the appeal processes, their 15-day deadline could conflict with the 60-day period under the NMC Act, potentially creating legal disputes that delay penal action. There is also a telling incident. As part of a proceeding under the RTI Act, the Central Information Commission revealed last year that the NMC had stated in 2024 that MARB had neither formally assessed nor rated medical colleges and that its standard forms need not be made public. In a revised reply in October 2025, it said the responding NMC officer’s records did not include any of the corresponding reports. However, the 2023 MARB regulations require the Board to publish its latest annual assessment results. If the NMC withdrew MSMER because the powers thereunder also exist elsewhere, the public deserves to know whether the powers are also being exercised and whether the outcomes are as publicly accessible as intended. Unless the NMC has satisfactory answers for all these lacunae, the withdrawal will appear less like simplification and more like regulatory relaxation.

articles.title: Wicked surprise: On the northeast monsoon
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: As India recovers from a monsoon-deficit year , there is both hope and trepidation regarding the prospects for that ‘other monsoon’, or the ‘northeast monsoon’ . While contributing only around a quarter of India’s annual rainfall, it is largely focused on the south-east peninsula regions of Tamil Nadu, Puducherry, coastal Andhra Pradesh, Rayalaseema, south interior Karnataka and Keralam. The southwest monsoon, influenced by a strengthening El Niño , has already left its desiccating mark. Rainfall from June-September was 759.4 mm against 868.6 mm, a 12.6% deficit, the driest in 11 years. This has impacted kharif sowing and is reflected in food inflation.

The India Meteorological Department (IMD) has said that this year, the northeast monsoon rainfall, spanning October to December, would likely be ‘normal’ , meaning in line with a 50-year average and within a 12% error window. Most parts of the country, it said, are expected to receive below-normal rainfall, except some areas of northwest India and southern parts of peninsular India, where rainfall is likely to be normal to above-normal. The wide error window, however, is far less precise than its forecasts for the southwest monsoon with its margin of 5%, and can sometimes make the northeast monsoon the bearer of nasty surprises. For instance, December 1, 2015, saw the city of Chennai deluged by its heaviest rainfall in 24-hours in over a century ; at least 500 lives were lost and 18 lakh people displaced in the State. That year and the present are linked by a common thread: a powerful El Niño. Associated with the heating up of the Central Pacific, the El Niño is linked to the drying up of the southwest monsoon rains but also yoked — not always — with a vigorous northeast monsoon. Other than in 2015, several El Niño years, such as 1997 and 2009, have been associated with above-normal rainfall between October and December in Tamil Nadu though El Niño years, such as 2002 and 1982, saw a poor northeast monsoon (and a predictably bad southwest monsoon). While the climate mechanisms linking a vigorous northeast monsoon and El Niño are still to be fully understood, it appears the warming patterns of the El Niño tend to deflect rain-bearing cyclonic circulations in unpredictable ways. Therefore, the Centre and the southern States ought to take enough precautions: from clearing up stormwater drains, fortifying shelters, making provisions for infrastructure damage and tightening weather warning forecasts to prepare for torrents.

articles.title: Old values, new avenues: On India-Poland ties
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: Sixteen years after his visit as Poland’s Prime Minister, Donald Tusk’s travel to Delhi and Bengaluru last week was to signal a renewed desire to work closely with India. Mr. Tusk’s visit, two months ahead of Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s trip to Brussels to sign the India-European Union (EU) Free Trade Agreement , indicated one part of his agenda. Both sides agreed that it was time to develop trade, currently worth just $6 billion, to double its size by 2030. Mr. Tusk’s last visit to India was in 2017, as President of the European Council for the EU-India summit, and it is fitting that his trip was just as the FTA is finalised and ratified after years of delays. Another area of increased India-Poland collaboration is in technology, AI and defence hardware, critical minerals, renewable and nuclear energy given Poland’s expertise in the last few decades and India’s capacity for scale. As the EU’s sixth largest economy, Poland has officially crossed the $1 trillion GDP (nominal terms) milestone. Its $120-billion-dollar tech economy is also gaining global interest. A large part of Polish machinery and parts is exported to Germany, which in turn has a growing share of Indian imports, and India could consider more trilateral collaborations for manufacturing and mining technology. The two sides agreed to establish a “Defence Industry Dialogue” and explore a dialogue on counter-terrorism cooperation. Finally, the Modi-Tusk talks focused on geopolitics, particularly the ongoing war in Ukraine. The war’s impact, especially on the Global South, has been a concern for India, and the Modi government’s initiative to work on an agreement acceptable to Kyiv and Moscow on grain exports and seafarers’ safety was discussed. The four-pronged plan, announced by External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar during his September visit to Warsaw, won Mr. Tusk’s support.

At the India-Poland Business Forum in Bengaluru, Mr. Tusk, who was accompanied by a Polish business delegation, said the challenge now was in “translating” the talks and MoUs signed into actual joint ventures between businesses. Apart from the distance and geographies, there is the matter of trust, given India’s defence engagement with Russia and Poland’s defence ties with Pakistan. Poland is credited with training Pakistan’s Air Force in its early years; a mutual defence cooperation agreement was signed in 2018. India has a unique and enduring partnership with Russia, and New Delhi is unlikely to accept Warsaw’s strictures over its military engagement and exercises with Russia that caused a controversy earlier this year during the Polish Foreign Minister’s visit. It is essential for Delhi and Warsaw to complete the confidentiality of classified information that is still being negotiated and draw up the parameters of future cooperation based on realities. Mr. Tusk’s statement that India and Poland today have no “conflicts of interest” is a significant aspiration, for two countries that share old values, and new avenues of partnership.

The two sides agreed to establish a “Defence Industry Dialogue” and explore a dialogue on counter-terrorism cooperation. Finally, the Modi-Tusk talks focused on geopolitics, particularly the ongoing war in Ukraine. The war’s impact, especially on the Global South, has been a concern for India, and the Modi government’s initiative to work on an agreement acceptable to Kyiv and Moscow on grain exports and seafarers’ safety was discussed. The four-pronged plan, announced by External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar during his September visit to Warsaw, won Mr. Tusk’s support.

Both sides agreed that it was time to develop trade, currently worth just $6 billion, to double its size by 2030. Mr. Tusk’s last visit to India was in 2017, as President of the European Council for the EU-India summit, and it is fitting that his trip was just as the FTA is finalised and ratified after years of delays. articles.title: In the crossfire: on India and the Saudi-Houthi conflict
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: The killing of an Indian national in a Houthi attack on Saudi Arabia’s Dammam airport is a grim reminder of the dangers the kingdom’s Indian community faces as the conflict between Riyadh and Yemen’s Shia militants escalates. Since the fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis resumed in July, at least two Indians have been killed and 14 others wounded. On Thursday, the Houthis claimed that a yacht with 14 Indians was targeted by Saudi forces near Yemen’s Zuqar island in the Red Sea and that rescue operations were under way. As the Houthis, who control parts of Northern Yemen and its entire Red Sea coast, step up attacks on Saudi infrastructure, including oil facilities and airports, Indians, who are the kingdom’s largest expat community, risk getting caught in the crossfire. With flights disrupted, thousands of Indian pilgrims are stranded. India has condemned Houthi attacks, saying that it “stands in solidarity” with Saudi Arabia. With no end in sight to the fighting and a high possibility of Israel and the U.S. resuming their Iran strikes, further violence and instability in West Asia could make India’s choices increasingly difficult.

The Saudi-Houthi conflict dates back to the Houthi takeover of Sana’a, Yemen’s capital, in 2014. A year later, Saudi Arabia began bombing Yemen to drive the Houthis out. But years of Saudi bombing of one of the poorest Arab countries have proved counterproductive; the Houthis consolidated support among the tribes of northern Yemen and built a powerful territorial army and naval force. The Saudi-Houthi ceasefire of 2022 collapsed in July 2026 after Saudi Arabia recklessly bombed Sana’a airport, to prevent an Iranian plane with a Houthi delegation from landing. The Houthis subsequently began attacking Saudi Arabia’s critical infrastructure, and launched a ground offensive against the Saudi-backed forces in Yemen. The Houthi attacks pose the biggest security challenge to Mohammed bin Salman, Saudi Arabia’s Crown Prince and the main architect of the war on Yemen, in decades. Massive Saudi air strikes have neither defeated the Houthis nor restored the kingdom’s deterrence. With its wealth, natural resources, infrastructure and tenuous palace politics, the kingdom remains exposed to Houthi missile and drone attacks, with few good options for a way out. India must prepare a contingency plan for worst-case scenarios. Its immediate priority should be to evacuate stranded Indian pilgrims. It should also articulate a stronger position for stability and work with Arab countries and Tehran to push for a diplomatic settlement to the Iran crisis . For peace to prevail in the Persian Gulf, the guns directed at Iran must first fall silent.
